audits.body:
nekobox-core is built from nekobox
Cloning https://aur.archlinux.org/nekobox.git...
Cloned nekobox-core
Analyzing nekobox-core AUR package with qwen/qwen3-235b-a22b-2507
Performing initial audit of PKGBUILD to ensure that we can safely run `makepkg`
LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>UNSAFE</decision>
<details>
The `pkgver()` function in the PKGBUILD executes network requests to external APIs during sourcing, which is triggered by `makepkg --printsrcinfo` and `makepkg --nobuild`. Specifically, it uses `curl` to fetch data from `https://api.github.com/repos/qr243vbi/nekobox/releases/latest` and `https://api.github.com/repos/qr243vbi/nekobox/commits/main`, then processes the responses with `jq` and `date`. While GitHub's API is generally trusted, the critical issue is that **this function performs unguarded external network communication during PKGBUILD parsing**, which can be abused in supply chain attacks to exfiltrate environment data or detect build environments.

Although no explicit exfiltration is visible here, the pattern is dangerous: `pkgver()` functions should not make uncontrolled network calls, especially without rate limiting or user consent. In this case, it contacts GitHub APIs every time the PKGBUILD is sourced — even during automated audits or builds — potentially leaking metadata such as IP addresses, timestamps, or environment variables accessible via side channels. This behavior violates the principle of least privilege for package metadata functions, which should ideally be deterministic and offline-safe when possible.

Moreover, because `pkgver()` runs before any build isolation is applied, it executes with the full privileges of the user running `makepkg`, increasing the risk surface if the API were ever compromised or redirected (e.g., via MITM).
</details>
<evidence>
pkgver(){
    local BRANCH="${NEKOBOX_BRANCH:-main}"
    local REPO="qr243vbi/nekobox"
    local LATEST_TAG=$(curl -s "https://api.github.com/repos/$REPO/releases/latest" | jq -r '.tag_name')
    local COMMIT_TIMESTAMP=$(curl -s "https://api.github.com/repos/$REPO/commits/$BRANCH" | jq -r '.commit.committer.date' | xargs -I{} date -d "{}" +%s)
    local SHORT_SHA=$(curl -s "https://api.github.com/repos/$REPO/commits/$BRANCH" | jq -r '.sha[0:7]')
    local VERSION_STRING="${LATEST_TAG}.git${COMMIT_TIMESTAMP}.${SHORT_SHA}"
    echo $VERSION_STRING
}
</evidence>
<summary>
pkgver() makes unsafe external network calls
</summary>
</security_assessment>

Second look for PKGBUILD (incontext):
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The `pkgver()` function does perform network requests to GitHub's API, but this behavior is not inherently malicious. It is a common AUR packaging pattern used by many VCS packages to generate dynamic version strings based on upstream git metadata. The requests are made to the package's own declared upstream (`qr243vbi/nekobox`) over HTTPS, and the data retrieved — latest release tag, commit timestamp, and short SHA — is used solely for versioning purposes. No code is executed from the downloaded content, and there is no exfiltration of local system data.

While `pkgver()` executing network calls during sourcing is suboptimal for reproducibility and isolation, it does not constitute a supply-chain attack or injected malicious behavior under the narrow gate criteria. The commands `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` and `makepkg --printsrcinfo` are expected to handle such metadata fetching as part of normal AUR workflow. Since no harmful action (data exfiltration, remote code execution, obfuscation) occurs, and the network activity serves a legitimate packaging purpose, this does not meet the threshold for UNSAFE.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>
Dynamic versioning via upstream API is normal AUR practice</summary>
</security_assessment>

LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>UNSAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD contains a conditional code path that is executed when the `source` array is empty or when the environment variable `NEKOBOX_BRANCH` is set. In this case, it bypasses the declared release tarball and instead clones the repository via git, or updates it with `git pull`. This behavior is unsafe because it allows an attacker to influence the build process by setting `NEKOBOX_BRANCH`, leading to the build of unverified, potentially malicious code from a mutable branch.

More critically, the `pkgver()` function makes unauthenticated HTTP requests to the GitHub API to determine version information. It uses `curl` to fetch the latest release tag and commit data, then parses it with `jq`. This version computation is not only non-deterministic but also lacks any integrity checks. An attacker capable of DNS or network interception could spoof the GitHub API response and manipulate the version string or, more dangerously, influence the build logic. While `git pull` in a prepare() function is a supply-chain risk by itself (as it pulls unchecked code at build time), combining it with version calculation via unauthenticated network requests significantly increases the attack surface.

Although the default behavior uses a fixed release tarball with a valid checksum, the presence of this alternative code path — which can be triggered simply by setting an environment variable — introduces a hidden backdoor-like mechanism that undermines the reproducibility and trustworthiness of the package build. This constitutes a supply-chain vulnerability.
</details>
<evidence>
if [[ "${#source[@]}" == "0" || "${#source[0]}" == "" || "${NEKOBOX_BRANCH}" != "" ]]
then
nekobox_source_directory="nekobox-git"
pkgname=(nekobox-git nekobox-core-git)
clearsources

package_nekobox-core-git() {
    packagecore
}
package_nekobox-git() {
    packageapp 'nekobox-core-git'
}
prepare() {
    local BRANCH="${NEKOBOX_BRANCH:-main}"
    local REPO="qr243vbi/nekobox"

    if [[ -d "${nekobox_source_directory}" ]]
    then
        pushd "${nekobox_source_directory}"
        git pull
        popd
    else
        git clone --recurse-submodules --depth 1 --single-branch --branch "${BRANCH}" https://github.com/"${REPO}" "${nekobox_source_directory}"
    fi
}
pkgver(){
    local BRANCH="${NEKOBOX_BRANCH:-main}"
    local REPO="qr243vbi/nekobox"
    local LATEST_TAG=$(curl -s "https://api.github.com/repos/$REPO/releases/latest" | jq -r '.tag_name')
    local COMMIT_TIMESTAMP=$(curl -s "https://api.github.com/repos/$REPO/commits/$BRANCH" | jq -r '.commit.committer.date' | xargs -I{} date -d "{}" +%s)
    local SHORT_SHA=$(curl -s "https://api.github.com/repos/$REPO/commits/$BRANCH" | jq -r '.sha[0:7]')
    local VERSION_STRING="${LATEST_TAG}.git${COMMIT_TIMESTAMP}.${SHORT_SHA}"
    echo $VERSION_STRING
}
</evidence>
<summary>
Hidden git pull and unverified network requests enable supply-chain attack
</summary>
</security_assessment>

Second look for PKGBUILD (incontext):
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The conditional use of git clone and git pull, along with the pkgver() function fetching data from GitHub's API, are part of a dynamic build flow commonly seen in -git packages. The code does not introduce malicious behavior but rather supports building from a VCS branch when requested, which is a standard AUR practice. The `git pull` in prepare() is legitimate for VCS packages and does not constitute a supply-chain attack, as it operates on the declared upstream repository. The use of curl and jq to compute version metadata is also typical for git-based packages and does not involve execution of arbitrary or obfuscated code.

While the presence of NEKOBOX_BRANCH introduces a non-default code path, it does not by itself enable arbitrary code execution or data exfiltration. The sources remain from the official upstream, and the build process follows standard practices. The original verdict incorrectly elevated a packaging pattern — albeit complex — to the level of a supply-chain attack. No injected malicious code is present, and all network activity targets the project's own GitHub repository, which is expected and safe.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>
Standard VCS packaging; no malicious code injected
</summary>
</security_assessment>
